A solvent is chosen in which the

steps.why: The method has no chemistry in it at all. It works only because the compound and the impurity dissolve to different extents in the same solvent, and because the compound is far more soluble hot than cold. Naming that difference is naming the principle.
common_mistakes: Saying crystallisation purifies liquids. It is a method for solids.
Saying it depends on the melting point. It depends on the solubility in a chosen solvent.
steps.memory_tip: The compound must dissolve much better hot than cold, and not in the same way as the impurity does.
steps.margin_note: Write the word SOLID and the word SOLUBILITY in the opening line. Those two words carry this mark.

The hot solution is filtered and set

lines.text: The impurities stay in the mother liquor

steps.why: The smallest quantity of hot solvent is used on purpose, so that the solution is close to saturated. On cooling, the compound is far past the quantity the cold solvent can dissolve and comes out as crystals, while the impurity is present in so small a quantity that the cold solvent still dissolves it.
common_mistakes: Using plenty of solvent. The smallest quantity that will dissolve the solid is used, so that cooling brings the compound out.
Saying the impurity is destroyed. It is not; it stays dissolved in the liquid left behind after the crystals are filtered off.
steps.memory_tip: Dissolve hot, cool, filter — and the liquid left over is the one carrying the impurities.
steps.margin_note: Name the mother liquor by that name. One closing line naming where the impurities go completes the answer.

insider_note: Two things carry this answer: the difference in solubility between compound and impurity in one solvent, and the sequence dissolve in the minimum of hot solvent, cool, filter. Naming the mother liquor is what says where the impurities went.
